# 1 Overview

## 1.1 Background

Housing plays a crucial role in shaping household wealth and social stability, serving as both a financial asset and a fundamental human necessity. In Singapore, where land scarcity and housing affordability are persistent public concerns, understanding the determinants of resale housing prices is particularly important for policy formulation and urban planning.

The price of a housing unit is influenced by a combination of structural and locational factors. Structural factors include intrinsic attributes such as floor area, flat type, lease remaining, and renovation quality, while locational factors capture the spatial context—such as accessibility to public transport, schools, and amenities.

Traditional modelling techniques, such as Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression, often fail to account for spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity inherent in housing data, leading to biased or inefficient estimates. To overcome these limitations, Geographically Weighted Models (GWMs) and other spatial econometric methods have been introduced to better capture local variations and spatial dependencies in housing markets.

## 1.2 The Task

This take-home exercise aims to build a spatially informed predictive model to estimate and predict HDB resale prices in Singapore. Using transaction data from July 2024 to June 2025, the task involves calibrating a predictive model capable of forecasting resale prices for the period July to September 2025.

The model should integrate appropriate geospatial analytical techniques to account for spatial patterns in housing prices, identifying both structural and locational determinants that influence resale value. Through this spatially enhanced approach, the analysis seeks to provide more accurate price predictions and deeper insights into the spatial dynamics of Singapore’s housing market.

# 2 Data import and data prepare

## 2.1 Data import

A total of 16 datasets were imported in this section, including both aspatial and spatial data. The imported datasets cover HDB resale transactions, urban planning boundaries, and various locational amenities such as schools, childcare centres, healthcare facilities, and public infrastructure.

Specifically, the aspatial dataset (HDBresale.csv) already filter 4-room flats between July 2024 and September 2025.

All other datasets were read and transformed into the Singapore SVY21 coordinate reference system (EPSG:3414) to ensure consistency for subsequent spatial analysis and distance computation.

In total: **1 aspatial dataset** (HDB resale). **15 spatial datasets**, including subzone boundaries, amenities (preschools, eldercare, hawker centres, parks, supermarkets, MRT and bus stations), educational institutions (kindergartens, childcare centres, clinics, primary schools, good schools), urban centres (CBD), and shopping malls.

## 2.2 OneMap Geocoding Function

This section performs geocoding using the Singapore OneMap API, transforming postal codes and address information into geographic coordinates for spatial analysis.

The function get_coords() was developed to batch-geocode postal codes for the schools, primary schools, and good primary schools datasets. It queries the OneMap endpoint to retrieve latitude and longitude, filters out invalid results, and converts the output into spatial features using the WGS84 coordinate system, later reprojected to SVY21 (EPSG:3414) for spatial consistency.

For the HDB resale dataset, the function geocode() was created to obtain coordinates based on the concatenation of block and street name. The retrieved coordinates were appended to each record, converting the aspatial HDB dataset into a spatial object. After transformation to the SVY21 projection, all datasets were spatially aligned for subsequent spatial analysis and modelling.

::: panel-tabset

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
get_coords <- function(search_list){
  
  coord_df <- data.frame()
  
  for (item in search_list){
    r <- GET('https://www.onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search?',
             query=list(searchVal=item,
                        returnGeom='Y',
                        getAddrDetails='Y'))
    data <- fromJSON(rawToChar(r$content))
    found <- data$found
    res <- data$results
    
    new_row <- data.frame()
    
    if (found == 1){
      new_row <- data.frame(
        search_val = item,
        postal = res$POSTAL,
        latitude = res$LATITUDE,
        longitude = res$LONGITUDE
      )
    }
    
    else if (found > 1){
      res_sub <- res[res$POSTAL != "NIL", ]
      
      if (nrow(res_sub) == 0){
        new_row <- data.frame(search_val = item,
                              postal = NA,
                              latitude = NA,
                              longitude = NA)
      } else {
        top1 <- head(res_sub, 1)
        new_row <- data.frame(
          search_val = item,
          postal = top1$POSTAL,
          latitude = top1$LATITUDE,
          longitude = top1$LONGITUDE
        )
      }
    }
    
    else {
      new_row <- data.frame(search_val = item,
                            postal = NA,
                            latitude = NA,
                            longitude = NA)
    }
    
    coord_df <- rbind(coord_df, new_row)
  }
  
  return(coord_df)
}
```

```{.r .cell-code}
geocode <- function(block, streetname) {
  base_url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"

  )

  output <- fromJSON(restext) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    select(results.LATITUDE, results.LONGITUDE)
  
  return(output)
}
```

## 2.7 MRT Geometry Correction

The MRT station dataset contained non-point geometries (e.g., polygons or mixed types). To correct this, the geometries were converted to point representations using a custom safe_point() function, which extracts the centroid or bounding box midpoint when errors occur.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sf_use_s2(FALSE)

mrt_station <- st_transform(mrt_station, 3414)
mrt_station <- st_zm(mrt_station, drop = TRUE, what = "ZM")

mrt_station <- st_collection_extract(mrt_station, "POLYGON", warn = FALSE)
mrt_station <- mrt_station[!st_is_empty(mrt_station), ]

safe_point <- function(g) {
  p <- try(st_point_on_surface(g), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(p, "try-error")) {
    bb <- st_bbox(g)
    st_point(c((bb["xmin"] + bb["xmax"]) / 2,
               (bb["ymin"] + bb["ymax"]) / 2))
  } else {
    st_geometry(p)[[1]]
  }
}

pts <- st_sfc(lapply(st_geometry(mrt_station), safe_point), crs = st_crs(mrt_station))
mrt_station <- st_set_geometry(mrt_station, pts)
mrt_station <- st_cast(mrt_station, "POINT", warn = FALSE)

# check result
unique(st_geometry_type(mrt_station))
```

## 4.2 Location factors

### 4.2.1 Calculate Nearest Distances

This step computes the Euclidean distance (in meters) from each HDB resale unit to the nearest key amenities and facilities, including the CBD, eldercare centres, hawker centres, MRT stations, parks, good primary schools, shopping malls, supermarkets, and clinics. The results are stored as new distance variables (e.g., dist_cbd, dist_mrt) to quantify locational accessibility.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# CBD
dis_cbd <- st_nearest_feature(HDBresale, cbd)
HDBresale$dist_cbd <- as.numeric(st_distance(HDBresale, cbd[dis_cbd, ], by_element = TRUE))

# Eldercare
dis_elder <- st_nearest_feature(HDBresale, eldercare)
HDBresale$dist_eldercare <- as.numeric(st_distance(HDBresale, eldercare[dis_elder, ], by_element = TRUE))

# Hawker
dis_hawker <- st_nearest_feature(HDBresale, hawker)
HDBresale$dist_hawker <- as.numeric(st_distance(HDBresale, hawker[dis_hawker, ], by_element = TRUE))

# MRT station
dis_mrt <- st_nearest_feature(HDBresale, mrt_station)
HDBresale$dist_mrt <- as.numeric(st_distance(HDBresale, mrt_station[dis_mrt, ], by_element = TRUE))

# parks
dis_parks <- st_nearest_feature(HDBresale, parks)
HDBresale$dist_park <- as.numeric(st_distance(HDBresale, parks[dis_parks, ], by_element = TRUE))

# Good primary schools
dis_goodps <- st_nearest_feature(HDBresale, good_primary_schools)
HDBresale$dist_good_primary <- as.numeric(st_distance(HDBresale, good_primary_schools[dis_goodps, ], by_element = TRUE))

# Shopping malls
dis_mall <- st_nearest_feature(HDBresale, shopping)
HDBresale$dist_mall <- as.numeric(st_distance(HDBresale, shopping[dis_mall, ], by_element = TRUE))

# Supermarkets
dis_super <- st_nearest_feature(HDBresale, supermarkets)
HDBresale$dist_supermarket <- as.numeric(st_distance(HDBresale, supermarkets[dis_super, ], by_element = TRUE))

# Clinics

HDBresale$dist_clinic <- as.numeric(st_distance(HDBresale, clinics[dis_clinic, ], by_element = TRUE))
```

For MLR, predictions are computed based on the global regression equation derived from the training data.

For gwRF, predictions are spatially adjusted using each observation’s coordinates (X, Y) with local and global weighting parameters (local.w=1, global.w=0), allowing the model to account for spatial heterogeneity and produce location-specific price estimates.

For the Random Forest (RF) model, predictions are generated using the ensemble of 500 decision trees trained on the full set of structural and locational features, enabling the model to capture complex nonlinear relationships between predictors and resale prices without considering spatial weighting.

## 9.3 Model Performance Comparison (RMSE)

This step evaluates and compares the predictive performance of the Multiple Linear Regression (MLR), Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR), Random Forest (RF), and Geographically Weighted Random Forest (gwRF) models using the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) metric, where lower values indicate higher prediction accuracy.

The results show that the GWR model (RMSE = 34,623.06) achieves the highest prediction accuracy, followed closely by the RF model (RMSE = 35,399.63) and the MLR model (RMSE = 77,431.47). In contrast, the gwRF model (RMSE = 155,659.39) performs significantly worse on the test dataset.

These findings suggest that accounting for spatial heterogeneity through GWR effectively improves predictive accuracy compared to the global MLR model, while the nonlinear ensemble structure of the RF also captures complex relationships between structural and locational factors well. However, the gwRF model underperforms—likely due to the suboptimal bandwidth selection—indicating that excessive localization in combination with nonlinear learning may have led to overfitting and unstable predictions. Overall, spatial effects in this dataset can be sufficiently explained by either local linear models (GWR) or global nonlinear models (RF), without the additional complexity introduced by gwRF.

# 10 Conclusion

This study examined the resale prices of 4-room HDB flats in Singapore from July 2024 to September 2025 using Multiple Linear Regression (MLR), Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR), Random Forest (RF), and Geographically Weighted Random Forest (gwRF) models. Structural attributes (e.g., floor area, storey level, remaining lease) and locational factors (e.g., distance to CBD, MRT, parks, and schools) were incorporated to assess their influence on price variation.

The MLR model achieved a strong fit (adjusted R² = 0.79) and reasonable accuracy (RMSE ≈ S\$77,431), but the Moran’s I test (0.327, p \< 0.001) revealed spatial autocorrelation in residuals, indicating that global linear assumptions could not fully capture spatial heterogeneity.

The GWR model effectively mitigated spatial dependence and achieved the lowest RMSE (≈ S\$34,623), showing that allowing coefficients to vary across space can better reflect local market dynamics.

The RF model also performed competitively (RMSE ≈ S\$35,400), capturing complex nonlinear relationships between structural and locational features. Spatial error visualization confirmed that the RF model generalizes well across Singapore — performing most accurately in the Central and East regions, while slightly underestimating prices in peripheral areas and marginally overestimating in the CBD and Queenstown.

The gwRF model, in theory, should outperform all other models by combining the spatial adaptivity of GWR with the nonlinear learning capacity of RF, thus reducing both spatial bias and global fitting errors. However, in this study, the gwRF model yielded higher RMSE (≈ S\$155,659) and right-skewed residuals, primarily due to suboptimal bandwidth selection and potential parameter interaction effects. These limitations likely caused over-localization and instability in predictions. Future research should refine the bandwidth optimization process, explore alternative kernel strategies, and consider larger or more diverse datasets to fully realize the theoretical potential of gwRF.

Overall, the results suggest that spatial heterogeneity in Singapore’s HDB resale market can be effectively explained by either local linear models (GWR) or global nonlinear models (RF). The RF model currently provides the best balance between predictive accuracy, robustness, and interpretability, while the gwRF framework remains a promising but computationally sensitive method deserving of further exploration.
